## Findings by module

### 2

- **refined** (ch-049 chunk 1 (colophon and Isaac the translator)): Budge's translation of the colophon: the book claims an Arabic version from a Coptic manuscript of the see of Mark, translated 'in the four hundred and ninth year of mercy' in the days of King Gabra Maskal (called Lalibala) and Abba George, and that Isaac the translator, with governor Ya'ebika Egzi'e's approval, put it into Ge'ez; he explains why earlier editors did not translate it in Zagwe times: it says non-Israelite kings transgress the Law. So the book openly attacks the Zagwe and favours the Solomonic restoration (Module 2 lesson 4), but its own colophon dates are unclear (era of mercy not converted here) and its provenance claim (Coptic and Arabic origin) is the compiler's. Index and verse list in chunk 2 are Budge's apparatus. Use as a politically motivated text and avoid a firm date for the compilation.
- **extended** (ch-008 and ch-009 (the Queen of Ethiopia, Tamrin, Solomon)): Budge's translation: the Queen of the South is identified with Ethiopia through the Gospel verse; she has ships, caravans and merchants (the merchant Tamrin loaded 520 camels and owned about 73 ships and supplied Solomon's temple building), she travels with 797 camels, worships the sun and other gods until she converts to the God of Israel; Solomon tricks her with salty food and an oath about water, and a dream says the sun of Israel went to Ethiopia. The story is a legitimising narrative with Christian commentary inserted by the compiler. It confirms the course's Module 2 lesson 4 reading of the Kebra Nagast as a political and religious text, not a record. Nothing in it is dated. Quote nothing.
- **extended** (ch-010 (the son, the ring, the succession law)): Budge's translation: the child is named Bayna-Lehkem (Menyelek), is sent at 22 with the merchant Tamrin and a ring as proof, the Queen decrees that only Solomon's male line shall rule and that sun and idol worship end; Solomon recognises his son, whose looks are said to match David's. The story explicitly creates a law of succession (formerly only a virgin woman could reign) and ties it to Zion. This is the text behind the Solomonic claim in Module 2 lesson 4; the compiler also adds New Testament commentary, so it is a later Christian composition, not an early document. Undated inside the text.
- **extended** (ch-011 (anointing as David, nobles' sons sent to Ethiopia)): Budge's translation: Solomon anoints his son in the temple and names him David; the sons of Israel's nobles go with him to found a second kingdom in Ethiopia; Zadok's blessings and curses repeat Deuteronomy. The text roots the Ethiopian monarchy in a covenant with Zion, a founding story for later kings' legitimacy [TRADITIONAL DATE]. Not evidence for any 10th-century BCE event.
- **extended** (ch-029 chunk 1 (Zion arrives in Ethiopia; oath on succession)): Budge's translation: the Ark ('heavenly Zion') arrives in Ethiopia by ship and the Queen builds a capital called Dabra Makeda; the nobles swear on Zion that only Solomon's male seed will reign and that women will never be queens; the people give up idols, augury and magic; Azariah is made chief priest. The Kebra Nagast thus supplies the oath behind the Solomonic restoration and also a prohibition of older religion (augury, charms), useful to show how a political text rewrites earlier Ethiopian religion. The sentence 'Dabra Makeda' and the sea route are narrative detail with no archaeological anchor [THIN EVIDENCE].
- **extended** (ch-029 chunk 2 (Azariah's speech, the name Makeda, Rome and Ethiopia)): Budge's translation: the Israelite priest says Ethiopia is 'better than Judah' and that God rejected Israel and chose Ethiopia; he mentions that the Ethiopians are 'black of face' without disparagement; the text gives food laws, bans augury and sun worship, explains the name Makeda ('Not thus'), and says the kings of Ethiopia and Rome were brethren in Christian faith until Rome fell to heresy (Nestorius, Arius). The compiler sets Ethiopia as the true Christian kingdom against Rome, so the Kebra Nagast is a Christian-era polemic about legitimacy and dated no earlier than the Christian Aksumite period; the Queen's boundaries run from Gaza and the Red Sea to the Sea of India [THIN EVIDENCE].
- **extended** (ch-029 chunk 3 (provenance claim: Hagia Sophia manuscript, council of bishops)): Budge's translation: the text claims it was found among manuscripts in the church of Sophia in Constantinople and approved by a council of 318 bishops (Domitius of Antioch, Gregory), who declare the king of Ethiopia the firstborn of Shem and more honourable than any king, with Rome second because of the Cross. This is the compiler's own provenance story, not a checked document; the course should teach it as a self-authenticating legitimising claim and not as evidence of a Greek origin [CONTESTED]. Reader and Diop both treat the Solomonic descent as a claim, not history.
- **extended** (ch-048 (Kaleb, Justin, Najran: a 6th-century anchor)): Budge's translation: the text names King Kaleb of Ethiopia and Justin of Rome as joint rulers who destroy the Jews of Najran and Armenia, and the Archbishop of Alexandria; it ends this section with Kaleb retiring to a monastery and his son Gabra Maskal succeeding. These names fit the historical Aksumite king Kaleb and the Najran events of the early 6th century CE (our inference, outside this book), which shows the text reuses real Aksumite history inside a legend. The narrative is placed in the 6th century but the whole book is a later compilation; do not date the compilation from these names.
- **note** (ch-047 (Zion stays in Ethiopia until the Last Day)): Budge's translation: the text says Ethiopia will never lose the Orthodox faith and that Zion (the Ark) will stay there until the end of the world, with harsh anti-Jewish judgment language. The anti-Jewish polemic is part of why the Kebra Nagast must be handled as a religious-political text; a lesson should note it without repeating it.
